To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) subjects' matching performances were affected by whether the stimuli consisted of one or two simultaneously presented forms; (b) subjects' matching accuracies were substantially lower when two simultaneously presented stimuli exerted discriminative control; (c) the matching accuracy declines appeared to reflect selective reductions in conditional stimulus control by the sample stimuli and shifts of control to the features of the comparison stimuli; (d) these findings challenge interpretations based on generalized stimulus control, shared attention, or stimulus generalization decrement; and (

the performance of retarded individuals on a visual matching-to-sample task can be affected substantially by the presence or absence of a second simultaneously displayed form, and that these effects can be explained by the operation of conditional control by the sample stimuli.

(1) the matching-to-sample performances that we obtained from subjects with mental retardations are consistent with the predictions of a theory based on conditional discrimination learning and stimulus control; (2) the matching performances that we obtained are not consistent with the predictions derived from stimulus generalization decrement and/or shared attention theories of matching; and (3) the performances that we observed from the subjects with mental retardaton are consistent with the results of research with nonhuman subjects.
